source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's SAT5-SAT6 campus in San Antonio publishes 33 MW of IT capacity across 175,000 square feet, and that is the whole of its published physical picture.

The certifications are the other half of what is published, and they read as a list of markets the campus is qualified to serve rather than a description of who is in it. SOC 2 Type 2 covers controls relevant to security and availability. PCI DSS covers payment card data. HIPAA and HITRUST cover protected health information. FISMA covers federal information systems. TIA-942 is a telecommunications infrastructure rating for the physical plant. None of these tells you which of those workloads is actually present.

The 33 MW figure is the number that matters for AI, and it needs one assumption to become concrete. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 33 MW of IT load is roughly 825 racks. That arithmetic is ours, not CyrusOne's, and the operator publishes no rack count, no accelerator count, and no density figure. The honest reading is that 33 MW is a mid-sized campus by the standards of the current buildout, large enough to host a meaningful training cluster and small enough that it is not, on its own, a frontier-scale site. Whether it hosts AI at all is not published.

In Texas, this campus ranks sixth by published megawattage among the 19 facilities in the state that publish a figure. Those 19 account for 475.41 MW, so SAT5-SAT6 is about 7 percent of the state's published capacity. Texas has 137 mapped facilities, which means the great majority publish no megawattage at all and the 475.41 MW total is a floor, not a census. A sixth-place ranking inside a partial count is a real position and a limited one. The campus matters as a qualified, powered, mid-sized node in the largest concentrated data center market in the country, and it does not, from anything published here, change the shape of the constraint.
